source_text: PAX ecce, dilectissimi fratres, Ecclesiae reddita est et, quod difficile nuper incredulis ac perfidis impossibile videbatur, ope atque ultione divina securitas nostra reparata est. In laetitiam mentes redeunt, et, tempestate pressurae ac nube discussa, tranquillitas ac serenitas refulserunt. Dandae laudes Deo, et beneficia ejus ac munera cum gratiarum actione celebranda, quamvis agere gratias nostra vox nec in persecutione cessaverit. Neque enim tantum inimico licere potest ut non, qui Dominum toto corde et anima et virtute diligimus, benedictiones ejus et laudes semper et ubique cum gloria praedicemus. Exoptatus votis omnium dies venit, et, post longae noctis horribilem tetramque caliginem, Domini luce radiatus mundus eluxit. Confessores, praeconio boni nominis claros et virtutis ac fidei laudibus gloriosos, laetis conspectibus intuemur, sanctis osculis adhaerentes, desideratos diu inexplebili cupiditate complectimur. Adest militum Christi cohors candida, qui persecutionis urgentus ferociam turbulentam stabili congressione fregerunt, parati ad patientiam carceris, armati ad tolerantiam mortis. Repugnastis fortiter saeculo, spectaculum gloriosum praebuistis Deo, secuturis fratribus fuistis exemplo. Religiosa vox Christum locuta est, in quem se semel credidisse confessa est. Illustres manus, quae non nisi divinis operibus assueverant, sacrificiis sacrilegis restiterunt. Sanctificata ora coelestibus cibis, post corpus et sanguinem Domini, profana contagia et idolorum reliquias respuerunt. Ab impio sceleratoque velamine, quo illic velabantur sacrificantium capita captiva, caput vestrum liberum mansit. Frons cum signo Dei pura, diaboli coronam ferre non potuit, coronae se Domini reservavit. Quam vos laete sinu suo excipit mater Ecclesia de praelio revertentes! quam beata, quam gaudens portas suas aperit, ut adunatis agminibus intretis, de hoste prostrato trophaea referentes! Cum triumphantibus viris et feminae veniunt, quae cum saeculo dimicantes, sexum quoque vicerunt. Veniunt et geminata militiae suae gloria virgines, et pueri annos suos virtutibus transeuntes. Necnon et caetera stantium multitudo vestram gloriam sequitur, proximis et pene conjunctis laudis insignibus vestigia vestra comitatur. Eadem et in illis sinceritas cordis, eadem fidei tenacis integritas. Inconcussis praeceptorum coelestium radicibus nixos et evangelicis traditionibus roboratos, non praescripta exilia, non destinata tormenta, non rei familiaris damna, non corporis supplicia terruerunt. Explorandae fidei praefiniebantur dies. Sed qui saeculo renuntiasse se meminit, nullum saeculi diem novit; nec tempora terrena jam computat qui aeternitatem de Deo sperat. Nemo, fratres dilectissimi, nemo hanc gloriam mutilet, nemo incorruptam stantium firmitatem maligna obtrectatione debilitet. Cum dies negantibus praestitutus excessit, quisquis professus intra diem non est, Christianum se esse confessus est. Primus est victoriae titulus, gentilium manibus apprehensum Dominum confiteri: secundus ad gloriam gradus est cauta secessione subtractum Domino reservari. Illa publica, haec privata confessio est. Ille judicem saeculi vincit, hic contentus Deo suo judice conscientiam puram cordis integritate custodit. Illic, fortitudo promptior, hic sollicitudo securior. Ille appropinquante hora sua, jam maturus inventus est; hic fortasse dilatus est qui, patrimonio derelicto, idcirco secessit quia non erat negaturus: confiteretur utique si fuisset et ipse detentus.
thought_title: Return of Peace to the Church
pass_a_gloss: Behold, most beloved brothers, peace has been restored to the Church and, what recently seemed impossible to unbelievers and the faithless, our security has been repaired by divine aid and vengeance. Minds return to joy, and, the storm of oppression and the cloud having been dispersed, tranquility and serenity have shone forth. Praises must be given to God, and His benefits and gifts must be celebrated with thanksgiving, although our voice did not cease to give thanks even in persecution. For not even the enemy can be allowed so much that we, who love the Lord with our whole heart and soul and strength, do not always and everywhere proclaim His blessings and praises with glory. The day longed for by all has come, and, after the horrible and dark night, the world has shone forth radiant with the Lord's light. We gaze upon the confessors, renowned for their good name and glorious for the praises of virtue and faith, with joyful countenances, adhering to them with holy kisses, embracing those long desired with insatiable longing. The white cohort of Christ's soldiers is present, who broke the fierce and turbulent fury of persecution with a stable confrontation, prepared for the patience of prison, armed for the tolerance of death. You resisted the world strongly, you presented a glorious spectacle to God, you were an example to subsequent brothers. The religious voice spoke Christ, in whom it confessed to have once believed. Illustrious hands, which were accustomed only to divine works, resisted sacrilegious sacrifices. Mouths sanctified by heavenly foods, after the body and blood of the Lord, rejected profane contagions and the remnants of idols. Your head remained free from the impious and wicked veil, with which the heads of those sacrificing were captive. Your forehead, pure with the sign of God, could not bear the devil's crown, it reserved itself for the Lord's crown. How gladly the mother Church receives you, returning from battle! How blessed, how rejoicing she opens her gates, so that you may enter with assembled troops, bringing back trophies from the prostrate enemy! Women come with the triumphant men, who, fighting with the world, also overcame their sex. Virgins also come, with double glory of their military service, and boys, surpassing their years with virtues. And also the rest of the multitude of those standing follows your glory, accompanying your footsteps with nearby and almost connected badges of praise. The same sincerity of heart and the same tenacity of faith are in them. Fixed on the unshaken roots of heavenly precepts and strengthened by evangelical traditions, they were not terrified by prescribed exiles, destined torments, losses of family, or bodily punishments. Days were being sought to test faith. But he who remembers that he has renounced the world knows no day of the world; nor does he compute earthly times, who hopes for eternity from God. No one, most beloved brothers, no one should mutilate this glory, no one should weaken the incorrupt firmness of those standing with malignant detraction. When the day appointed for those denying has passed, whoever has not professed within the day has confessed himself to be a Christian. The first title of victory is to confess the Lord, apprehended by the hands of Gentiles; the second step to glory is to be reserved for the Lord by cautious secession. The former is public, the latter private confession. The former conquers the judge of the world, the latter, content with his own judge, God, keeps a pure conscience with the integrity of heart. There, fortitude is more prompt; here, solicitude is more secure. He, whose hour was approaching, was already found mature; the other, perhaps delayed, who, having abandoned his patrimony, withdrew because he was not going to deny: he would certainly have confessed if he had also been detained.

pass_b_english: Behold, dearest brothers, peace has returned to the Church, and our safety has been restored by God’s help and vengeance—a thing that recently seemed impossible to unbelievers and the faithless. Joy returns to our minds, and now that the storm of oppression has broken and the cloud has scattered, tranquility and serenity shine forth. We must give praise to God and celebrate his benefits and gifts with thanksgiving, even though our voice never stopped giving thanks even during the persecution. For the enemy cannot be allowed such power that we, who love the Lord with all our heart and soul and strength, would not always and everywhere proclaim his blessings and praises with glory. The day everyone longed for has arrived, and after the horrible, dark night, the world has shone radiant with the Lord’s light. We look upon the confessors, renowned for their good name and glorious for the praises of virtue and faith, with joyful faces; we cling to them with holy kisses and embrace those we have longed for with an insatiable desire. The white cohort of Christ’s soldiers stands here, those who broke the fierce and turbulent fury of persecution by standing firm, prepared for the patience of prison and armed for the endurance of death. You resisted the world bravely, you gave God a glorious spectacle, and you became an example for the brothers who would follow. The religious voice confessed Christ, in whom it confessed it had once believed. Illustrious hands, accustomed only to divine works, refused to take part in sacrilegious sacrifices. Mouths sanctified by heavenly food, after receiving the body and blood of the Lord, rejected profane contagions and the remnants of idols. Your heads remained free from the impious, wicked veil that covered the captive heads of those who sacrificed. Your foreheads, pure with the sign of God, could not bear the devil’s crown; they reserved themselves for the Lord’s crown. How gladly mother Church welcomes you as you return from battle! How blessed and joyfully she opens her gates so that you may enter with assembled ranks, bringing back trophies from the prostrate enemy! Women come with the triumphant men, who, while fighting the world, also conquered their own sex. Virgins come as well, bearing a double glory of their warfare, and boys who surpass their years with virtues. The rest of the multitude of those standing also follows your glory, accompanying your footsteps with badges of praise that are near and almost joined to your own. The same sincerity of heart and the same tenacity of faith are in them. Fixed on the unshaken roots of heavenly precepts and strengthened by evangelical traditions, they were not terrified by prescribed exiles, destined torments, loss of property, or bodily punishments. Days were being set to test their faith. But whoever remembers that he has renounced the world knows no day of the world; nor does he calculate earthly times, he who hopes for eternity from God. No one, dearest brothers, no one should mutilate this glory; no one should weaken the incorrupt firmness of those who stand with malignant detraction. When the day appointed for those who denied has passed, whoever did not profess within that day has confessed himself to be a Christian. The first title of victory is to confess the Lord, seized by the hands of the Gentiles; the second step toward glory is to be reserved for the Lord by a cautious withdrawal. The former is public confession, the latter private. The former conquers the judge of the world; the latter, content with God as his judge, keeps a pure conscience with integrity of heart. There, fortitude is more prompt; here, solicitude is more secure. The one whose hour was approaching was already found mature; the other, perhaps delayed, who abandoned his patrimony, withdrew because he was not going to deny—he certainly would have confessed if he had also been detained.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin. Specific nuances such as 'ope atque ultione divina' (by divine aid and vengeance) and the distinction between 'illa publica, haec privata confessio' (the former is public, the latter private) are correctly rendered. The translation of 'non rei familiaris damna' as 'losses of family' (A) and 'loss of property' (B) are both acceptable interpretations of the Latin regarding family/estate matters.
